## Frustration is part of learning R, but it doesn't have to be


-   You will get errors (need fixing) and warnings (just informative) when you run code
-   Errors and warnings are your friends. They tell you what is wrong

. . .

-   **Errors and warnings are not your fault. They are part of the learning process**

. . .

-   Take a breath and step away
-   Work on it for a set time; don't go down a rabbit hole
-   When you're more settled ...

## Trying to figure it out

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Check the documentation of the function you are using (`?function_name` or `help(function_name)`)
-   Approach the problem from a different angle
-   Ask for help from the local community (classmates, instructor)
-   Consult online resources (Stack Overflow, RStudio Community, Claude AI)

:::

## What is coding?

-   Translating a set of logical steps into a language the computer understands
    -   It is a "conversation" with a computer (no, we're not going to vibe code here)
    -   using a grammar and vocabulary that the computer understands[^1]

::: incremental
- Computers are "dumb" - they do exactly what you tell them to do
    - Things can get lost in translation
    - So you have to be accurate and precise
    - If the computer is making a mistake, it's because of the instructions it got
    - You have to tell it everything, even the things that seem obvious to you (but it gets better)
:::

[^1]: So you'll get into similar difficulties as asking directions in Tokyo or Paris.
    
## An opinionated tour of {{< fa brands r-project >}}

- We will concentrate on  the tidyverse set of packages 
    - So you don't have to tell R everything
    - Reasonable choices have been made for you
- We won't learn everything today
    - You will learn more as you go along
    - You will learn more by doing
    - You will learn more by making mistakes and getting feedback

# Start up R and RStudio

{{< countdown minutes="1" >}}

## Make an RStudio project
- Projects help you manage your work
- They keep your files organized
- They help R find your files

If you create a project, and then forget where you created it, type `getwd()` in the console to find out where you are. 

For reference, you can see a walkthrough of creating a project [here](https://www.araastat.com/BIOF339/slides/lectures/week5/01-best_practices.html#14).

## Basic keyboard shortcuts

::: callout-note
## Regular coding use keyboard shortcuts
- Run current line or selection: {{< kbd "Ctrl+Enter" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+Enter" >}} (Mac)
- Insert assignment operator: {{< kbd "Alt+-" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Option+-" >}} (Mac)
- insert pipe operator: {{< kbd "Ctrl+Shift+M" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+Shift+M" >}} (Mac)

- Comment/uncomment current line or selection: {{< kbd "Ctrl+Shift+C" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+Shift+C" >}} (Mac)
:::

::: callout-note
## General use keyboard shortcuts

- Find: {{< kbd "Ctrl+F" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+F" >}} (Mac)
- Replace: {{< kbd "Ctrl+H" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+Option+F" >}} (Mac)
- Save: {{< kbd "Ctrl+S" >}} (Windows) or {{< kbd "Cmd+S" >}} (Mac)
:::

# Packages

## What are packages?
- Packages are collections of R functions, data, and compiled code in a well-defined format
  - Usually for a specific purpose
  - They extend R's functionality
- R comes with a standard set of packages, but there are thousands more available
  - You can install packages from CRAN, Bioconductor, GitHub, and other repositories

::: callout-note
Packages are collections of functions, and sometimes data, that are usually unified for a common purpose

If functions are recipes, then packages are recipe books

If you want to cook from a recipe, you first have to grab the recipe book from your shelf

[Similarly, if you want to use a function from a package, you first have to grab or activate the package in your current R session]{style="color: red; font-weight: bold;"}
:::

An (incomplete) list of packages you might want to explore is available [here](https://www.araastat.com/BIOF339/slides/lectures/week2/01-packages.html#17)

## Installing and loading packages

::: callout-important
You only need to install a package once, but you need to load it every time you start a new R session
:::

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

::: callout-note
If you don't have the package `janitor` installed, you can install it by running the following command once:
```r
install.packages("janitor")
```
{{< countdown seconds="45" minutes="0">}}
:::

## Using functions from packages

There is another way to access functions from packages, if you're really only going to use one function from it.

The general form for this is `<package>::<function>` (note the two colons)

For example, if you just want to use the `clean_names` function from the **janitor** package, you can do so by

```r
janitor::clean_names(dataset)
```

where dataset is the name of the data.frame whose column names you want to clean.

## Cleaning names (to maintain sanity and typing efficiency) {background-image="https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/79a12c01-0cc1-4643-b1e7-8ce8cafc947b_rw_1200.png?h=4136fa7e5c95e6d8e4b3a35faaebd082" background-size="contain" background-repeat="no-repeat" background-position="center:center"
}

## Cleaning names (to maintain sanity and typing efficiency)

```{webr}
library(readr)
library(janitor)

cars <- read_csv("data/cars2018.csv")
# cars <- janitor::clean_names(cars)
head(cars)
```

::: {.aside}
The dataset is available [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gu-dsan5200/datasets/refs/heads/main/cars2018.csv)
:::

::: callout-important
If you download the data, you **need to know** where it's downloaded to on your computer, so that you can tell R where to find it. 
Typically this is your "Downloads" folder. Preferably, you move it to your project's `data` folder.
:::

{{< countdown minutes="1" seconds="30" >}}

## Easier data imports: the `rio` package

- Install the **rio** package if you haven't already

{{< countdown seconds="60" minutes="0">}}

## Now use it 

```{webr}
library(rio)

cars <- import("data/cars2018.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() ## what's going on here?
head(cars)
```

`janitor::clean_names()` calls the `clean_names` function from the **janitor** package, without loading the whole package

But what is this `|>` thing? (I create this using {{< kbd "Ctrl+Shift+M" >}} or {{< kbd "Cmd+Shift+M" >}})

## Pipes

Pipes are a method in R to create analytic pipelines utilizing tidyverse functions.

The pipe operator (denoted `|>`, spoken as "going to") is what creates the pipes.

You start with a dataset, and then progressively add functions to the pipe. Typically you save the result to a new object.

Each element of the pipe takes as its first argument the results of the previous step, which typically is a data frame.

Pipes are just a different representation of an analytic process that we can do in separate steps anyway. We'll see this later.
